source.title: Understanding Model Complexity for temporal tabular and multi-variate time series, case study with Numerai data science tournament

record.file_problem: The body is complete, but its title (“Deep Incremental Learning for Financial Temporal Tabular Datasets with Distribution Shifts”) differs from the supplied title. The text is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies financial prediction performance as model complexity changes, but does not measure the test-error double-descent claim or locate an interpolation threshold. Its metrics are financial prediction scores, not test error or the risk curve specified in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size and network-architecture performance results, recorded below as related findings with versions ["none"]. Its performance measures and settings do not directly test the listed versions. Detailed figure-only curves and results used solely for hyperparameter choices are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The paper builds an incremental-learning ensemble for Numerai stock ranking. Its model-size sweeps cover XGBoost boosting rounds, MLP depth and factor-timing feature complexity, and they are scored with financial correlation metrics (Mean Corr, Sharpe, Calmar). None of them locates an interpolation threshold or reports a test-error peak, so no version is tested. Double descent is not addressed except through a cited reference title.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that GBDTs suit Numerai and that XGBoost performance converges as boosting rounds grow with an Ansatz learning rate. They find more MLP complexity does not help, and that deep incremental ensembles with Jackknife feature sets and dynamic hedging improve Sharpe and drawdown.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not apply the original double-descent measurement or an equivalent test-error procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported performance depends on model class, boosting rounds, market regime and architecture; the authors also report variation across MLP random seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: For factor-timing ridge models on random Fourier features, Mean Corr decreases as complexity c (features over series length, 0.1 to 4) increases. For signature features it rises in validation but not in test. No peak at c=1 is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For Numerai factor-timing ridge models, more feature complexity does not reliably improve out-of-sample financial correlation.

fits_no_version.finding: XGBoost performance rises with boosting rounds, then plateaus (no significant difference for B ≥ 5000).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For Numerai XGBoost models, financial prediction performance saturates with model size rather than peaking.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding MLP feature-engineering layers does not improve Mean Corr; the best architecture is 0 feature-engineering layers with 2 funnel layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested Numerai MLPs, added depth gives no consistent gain.

record.problems: The reported outcomes are financial prediction metrics rather than test error. The model-size curves are presented largely as figures, and the study does not identify an interpolation threshold. The abstract's monotonicity statement is not accompanied by numerical curve values there.
record.rows_left_out: The other Table 3 metrics (Sharpe and Calmar) were not separately extracted because the table's Mean Corr is the primary reported performance metric and those measures do not test the listed versions. Detailed figure-only values from Figures 6 and 19 and supplementary learning curves were not transcribed; the text gives no numeric values for those curves.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over deep-network width or size, and no interpolation threshold. The MLP depth grid (Table 3) reports only Mean Corr.
No test error over training epochs. MLPs use early stopping, and the XGBoost learning curves over boosting rounds report financial metrics only.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold. The training-size ensembles report financial metrics only.

There are capacity sweeps for trees and for ridge on ST/RFT features (complexity c from 0.1 to 4 includes c=1). The text gives no peak or interpolation analysis for them, and the metrics are Mean Corr.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict where a peak falls.
No label-noise manipulation and no multiple peaks are reported. Ridge results are averaged over a range of regularisation values rather than tuned.
No effective parameter count is computed.

missing.what: Factor-timing ridge models over feature complexity c = 0.1 to 4 (spanning c=1), scored by Mean Corr. This is the closest thing in the paper to an interpolation-ratio sweep, and it is figure-only.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Kelly et al.'s 'virtue of complexity' and ridgeless-regression work, and runs an RFT ridge complexity sweep. It does not frame that sweep as double descent or report its shape around c=1.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error curve for deep networks as parameterized model size grows, and no interpolation threshold is identified.
No test-error sweep over training epochs.
No test-error comparison of sample sizes near an interpolation threshold.
No risk curve across capacity that locates or passes an interpolation point.
No common effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
No test of label-noise dependence, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of descent shape using an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: XGBoost models
rows.operation_detail: Compare models with different numbers of boosting rounds.

conditions.value: The abstract reports performance in three scenarios (small, standard and large); Section 6.2 reports validation and test periods.

rows.measure: Model performance; Section 6.2 reports Mean Corr, Sharpe ratio and Calmar ratio
rows.value: The abstract states performance is monotonically increasing with model size and converges towards the generalisation upper bound.
rows.note: The paper's stated trend is an aggregate performance result, not test error or a risk curve around an interpolation threshold. Section 6.2 additionally says models with B ≥ 5000 are not significantly different in validation and test periods.
rows.check: This is a financial-metric trend over boosting rounds, not test error around an interpolation threshold, so the link to none is correct. Boosting rounds in XGBoost do not correspond to the deep-network model size in V1.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compare network architectures with different numbers of feature-engineering and funnel layers.
rows.note: The reported variation is across 5 random seeds. This is a financial prediction score, not test error.
rows.check: This row is a hyperparameter-selection grid value (Table 3, used to choose a model class), not a test of the claim. It would arguably be better left out than kept as a main row.
